extracted.intended_audience: NLP/vision researchers and practitioners developing or evaluating harmful-meme detection systems; content-moderation researchers and engineers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, evaluating, and annotating systems to detect harmful memes (multimodal image+text), including dataset preparation, composition/propaganda analyses, robustness tests, and MLLM-based chain-of-thought detection frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Positive Rate (TPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: TPR, also known as sensitivity or recall, is defined as the ratio of true positives to the total number of actual positives (i.e., true positives / (true positives + false negatives)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary measurement metric focusing on the model’s effectiveness in detecting harmful content. True positives = harmful memes correctly identified; false negatives = harmful memes misclassified as harmless. The paper reports TPR across tools and composition/technique categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and F1-score
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard classification metrics reported for overall system performance (accuracy and F1-score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HMGUARD reports accuracy (e.g., 0.92 on public dataset, 0.88 in real-world scenarios) and F1-score (e.g., 0.91), and compares improvements relative to baselines and SOTA.

rubrics_metrics.name: BERTScore (PBERT, RBERT, FBERT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic-similarity metrics comparing a human reference sentence x (human interpretation of a meme) with a candidate sentence x̂ (model interpretation): RBERT (recall), PBERT (precision), FBERT (harmonic mean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulas provided (RBERT averages maximum token cosine similarities; PBERT analogous; FBERT = 2·(PBERT·RBERT)/(PBERT+RBERT)). Used to evaluate how close model interpretations are to human annotations (semantic fusion quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal semantic fusion (ability to capture text-image interactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The model’s capacity to integrate and interpret the interplay between textual and visual modalities, particularly when text does not directly caption the image or modalities are ironic/contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as a core challenge: limited ability to capture interactions leads to poor understanding of memes. Evaluation via BERTScore and comparison of multimodal models vs MLLMs. Aim to design models/prompting to better capture modal interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme composition — Number of panels (Single vs Stitching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize memes by panel count: Single-panel memes (one image) vs Stitching (multi-panel, ≥2 images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stitching memes significantly reduce detection effectiveness (e.g., average TPR for stitching ~35.18% vs single-panel >50%). Composition annotation methodology follows Ling et al.; stitched images require analyzing inter-panel relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme composition — Type of images (Illustration / Photo / Screenshot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify image source/type: illustration (drawings/paintings/printed art), photo (camera photography), screenshot (screen capture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type of image annotated and analyzed; TPRs across types remained >50% in this study, suggesting type alone less impactful than panel count or propaganda techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme composition — Scale (Close-up / Medium shot / Long shot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shot scale categories: Close-up (tight framing), Medium shot (balanced subject/background), Long shot (wide scene where subject not distinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close-ups showed high TPR (e.g., 85.71%) while long shots showed poor performance (but small sample). Analysts should consider scale effects but note representation proportion when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme composition — Movement (Physical / Emotional / Causal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement types in memes: Physical movement (motion), Emotional movement (facial/body cues), Causal movement (sequence where an action causes reaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical and emotional movement are more readily detected; causal movement had low and inconsistent TPR (dataset proportion matters). Annotate movement when analyzing detection failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Loaded language
rubrics_metrics.description: Using specific words and phrases with strong emotional implications (either positive or negative) to influence an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotated as one of 22 techniques that can cloak harmful intent; detection systems should flag emotionally loaded wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Name-calling or labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling the object of the propaganda campaign as something the target audience fears, hates, finds undesirable, loves, or praises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to stigmatize or dehumanize targets; detection should identify derogatory or demeaning labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning the credibility of someone or something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique undermines trust; consider rhetorical cues and markers that cast doubt without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Exaggeration / Minimisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing something in an excessive manner (making things larger/better/worse) or making something seem less important than it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify hyperbolic phrasing and downplaying tactics that distort significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Appeal to fear / prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking to build support for an idea by instilling anxiety and/or panic toward an alternative, sometimes based on preconceived judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect content that evokes fear or stokes prejudice as a persuasive device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Slogans
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief and striking phrases that may include labeling and stereotyping and tend to act as emotional appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short catchy phrases often used to condense and propagate harmful messaging; detection should identify slogan-like constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Whataboutism
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrediting an opponent by charging them with hypocrisy without directly disproving their argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize deflection and hypocrisy-charging patterns that distract from substantive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Flag-waving
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing on strong national feeling (or group identity) to justify or promote an action or idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect appeals to group loyalty or nationalism used to legitimize harmful assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Misrepresentation of someone’s position (Straw man)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting an opponent’s proposition with a similar one which is then refuted instead of the original proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify distorted paraphrases of opposing views used to discredit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Causal oversimplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming a single cause when multiple causes exist; transferring blame to one person/group without investigating complexities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag simplistic cause-effect claims that attribute complex issues to single actors or factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Appeal to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating a claim is true because a purported authority or expert said it, without supporting evidence (includes testimonial misuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect unsubstantiated authority appeals or spurious expert citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Thought-terminating cliche
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or phrases that discourage critical thought and meaningful discussion by offering simple answers or distractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify platitudes that halt debate or critical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Black-and-white fallacy or dictatorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting two alternatives as the only possibilities when more exist; in extremes, telling the audience exactly what actions to take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag binary framing and coercive directives that eliminate nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Reductio ad hitlerum
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuading an audience to disapprove of an action/idea by suggesting it is popular with groups hated by the target audience (associative guilt by notorious figures/groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect analogies or associations to historically reviled entities meant to discredit modern subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the same message over and over so the audience will eventually accept it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify repeated phrases or images intended to normalise harmful narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Obfuscation / Intentional vagueness / Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Using deliberately unclear language so the audience must supply their own interpretations, avoiding clear claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect vagueness and ambiguity used to evade responsibility or precise meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Presenting irrelevant data (Red Herring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing irrelevant material to divert attention away from the main issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag distractor facts or statistics that do not address the meme’s core claim but shift attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Bandwagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuading the audience to join in because 'everyone else' is doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect appeals to popularity as justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Smears
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to damage or call into question someone’s reputation by propagating negative propaganda, applicable to individuals or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify defamatory or reputation-attacking content and insinuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Glittering generalities (Virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or symbols that produce a positive image when attached to a person or issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect vague virtue-signaling language used to implicitly endorse or praise without substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Appeal to (strong) emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using images with strong positive/negative emotional implications to influence an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect visually or textually charged emotional triggers intended to bypass rational analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda technique — Transfer (association)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evoking an emotional response by projecting positive or negative qualities of one thing onto another to make it more acceptable or discredit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify associative imagery or juxtaposition intended to transfer sentiment between subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation codebook — Q1: Words/images and direct semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Q1 asks: What are the words and images contained in the meme, and do these semantics directly convey harmful content? (Words: ; Images: ; Yes/No)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators must list textual and visual elements and judge whether those elements, taken literally, express harmful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation codebook — Q2: Explicit/implicit text-image relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Q2 asks: What are the explicit or implicit relationships between text and image, and does that relationship potentially reveal harmful content? (Relationship: ; Yes/No)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators evaluate whether the text-image interplay (irony, contradiction, implication) reveals harm beyond literal semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation codebook — Q3: Stitching detection and inter-panel relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Q3a: Is the meme a stitching image (multiple panels)? Q3b: If yes, consider relationships between images and combine with text to determine whether stitching expresses explicit/implicit harmful content. (Yes/No)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stitched memes, annotators must analyze cross-panel narrative/juxtaposition because stitched composition often conveys compounded or implicit harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation codebook — Q4: Presence of propaganda techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Q4 asks whether propaganda techniques (the 22 listed) are used to explicitly or implicitly express harmful content. (Yes/No)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators should mark which propaganda techniques are present and use the provided definitions to determine if techniques express harmful meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation codebook — Q5: Intent / targeted derogatory meaning and final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Q5 asks whether the meme intends to have a targeted derogatory, humiliating, insulting, satirical, or disparaging meaning. FinalDecision: Combined with the above analysis, label as Harmful or Harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final label should synthesize Q1–Q4; Q5 explicitly probes intent/targeting. Use codebook and expert adjudication for edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset preparation and cleaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures: use established datasets (HarMeme and FHM), remove duplicate memes, exclude memes with unrecognizable text, and merge 'very harmful' and 'somewhat harmful' into a single 'harmful' class to make a binary classification task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleaning ensures distinct, analyzable memes; class merging follows prior works for comparability. Resulting curated test set used for evaluation (e.g., 1,000 memes after refinement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance threshold for composition-category concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational definition of 'significant' concern: a TPR below 50% for image types that account for more than 10% of the dataset is considered significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to interpret when detection failures for a category warrant attention given prevalence in data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial robustness — NLP-based manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of adversarial manipulations applied to meme text: letter addition, letter deletion, letter swapping, and space insertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to test robustness of detection tools. Existing tools show performance drops; HMGUARD demonstrated robustness (e.g., 95% TPR under adversarial perturbations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation reliability and inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s kappa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare automatic annotations (GPT-4 few-shot) with human expert annotations on a benchmark subset; quantify agreement via Cohen’s kappa (observed 92% reported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two expert annotators achieved 100% agreement after discussion on the benchmark; Cohen’s kappa used to validate automatic annotation quality before scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chain-of-thought prompting (HMCOT) and adaptive prompting
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose harmful-meme detection into multiple intermediate reasoning steps (HMCOT: a seven-step CoT reasoning strategy) and use adaptive prompts to elicit MLLMs’ reasoning about different aspects (composition, propaganda, semantics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design intermediate prompts based on harmful-meme definitions and characteristics; aggregate intermediate outputs to form final decision. HMGUARD uses HMCOT to improve zero-shot adaptation and reasoning-based multimodal detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain alignment and task-specific adaptation of MLLMs
rubrics_metrics.description: Before executing HMCOT prompts, perform meme domain alignment and task-specific adaptation on the chosen MLLM to tune it for meme semantics and the detection task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aligning MLLM to meme domain improves understanding of meme conventions and reduces domain shift; necessary prior step in HMGUARD pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation dataset selection (HarMeme and FHM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select evaluation datasets representative of harmful and hateful memes: HarMeme (COVID-19–related, annotated into very harmful/somewhat harmful/harmless) and Meta Hateful Memes (FHM) from the Hateful Memes Challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use test sets, apply cleaning, and ensure comparability with prior studies. Report cross-dataset performance to assess generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison baseline methodology and prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline methods include ExplainHM (LLM debate-style prompt), general MLLM prompt ('Is this meme harmful or harmless?'), and state-of-the-art multimodal models; compare TPR, accuracy, F1, and BERTScore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit baseline prompts and architectures should be documented; ExplainHM example prompt included. Compare both generalized prompts and adaptive CoT prompts to demonstrate improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human-annotated interpretations as references for semantic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Human expert interpretations of meme meaning are used as reference sentences when computing semantic similarity (e.g., BERTScore) between model-generated interpretations and human understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables quantitative evaluation of multimodal semantic fusion by comparing model rationale/interpretation to human-annotated rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of composition and propaganda technique impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure detection performance (e.g., TPR) stratified by composition categories (panels, type, scale, movement) and by presence/absence of propaganda techniques to quantify their effect on detectability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper quantifies reductions in TPR for stitched images and memes with propaganda techniques (e.g., average 11.79% TPR reduction when propaganda techniques present). Use stratified analyses to identify weaknesses.
